For two months after the breakup, Vishal slept badly and snapped at everyone at work. He knew he needed someone to talk to. He also knew his savings were thin after paying for his sister's college admission.

At lunch, Ujjwal mentioned, as casually as if he were talking about the dentist, that he saw a counsellor every other Thursday. "Keeps the engine running," he said.

That evening Vishal searched and found two things: private therapists whose fees he couldn't manage right now, and a training clinic at the university's psychology department, where supervised counsellors charged according to income. There was a three-week wait.

He booked it anyway. He also joined a free weekly peer group run by a local volunteer centre, just to have somewhere to go in the meantime.

On the first Thursday, he sat in the waiting room with his knee jiggling. When the counsellor called his name, he stood up quickly, before he could change his mind.

qa.a: At a training clinic at the university's psychology department, where supervised counsellors charged according to income.

The family lunch in Andheri was going well until Yash's phone buzzed with a reminder: Session, 5 p.m.

"Session of what?" his uncle asked.

"Therapy," Yash said, passing the raita. "Once a month."

His uncle put down his spoon. "Therapy? Is something wrong with you?"

"Nothing's wrong. I go to the gym for my back. I go to the counsellor for my head. It's maintenance."

A short silence. His aunt changed the subject to mangoes.

Later, on the balcony, his cousin Asif came out with two cups of tea. "Was that true? Just maintenance?"

"Mostly. When work gets bad, it helps to have someone who already knows the story."

Asif stared at the traffic. "My exams stuff is getting to me. How do I even find someone?"

"Check they're properly qualified, and meet one or two before you decide. If it doesn't feel right, try someone else. I'll send you where I started."

The campaign brief came in on a Monday: a skin-whitening cream, and I was the lead copywriter. I read the words "brighter, fairer, more confident" and felt my stomach turn.

My sister had spent her teens being compared with fairer cousins. I was the one who told her she was beautiful exactly as she was. And now I was supposed to sell the opposite.

But I'm also the one who pays my parents' rent. Quitting on principle was not a real option.

I talked to Pema, our creative director, that afternoon. I said, "I'll work on anything else, double if needed, but I can't write this one and still look my sister in the eye." I expected a lecture. Pema just said, "Thank you for telling me early," and moved me to a school-uniform account.

Looking back, I'm Wasim, a copywriter who needs this job, and a brother who meant what he said. That day, I didn't have to choose only one.

qa.a: The brief was for a skin-whitening cream, with Wasim as lead copywriter.

Note, Saturday. Parveen, my former student, came to see me at the college about her future.

Her father wants her to join the family hardware shop in Bhopal. She has spent five years training as an architect and wants to design low-cost homes. She said, "Everyone makes it sound like I have to choose between being a good daughter and being an architect."

I asked her what she actually valued in each. She thought for a long time. The shop, she said, was about her father's pride and the customers who had trusted him for thirty years. Architecture was about making homes people could afford.

Then she laughed, surprised. "The shop sells building materials. Half its customers are building homes."

By the end she had a draft plan: work at a firm on weekdays, help at the shop on Saturdays, and start a small design desk inside the shop for local builders.

I told her to show her father the plan, not just the problem.

— Avni

Taught Class 8 about soil today and, halfway through, realised I was talking about our own fields. The children leaned in. That never happens with textbook examples.

Appa wants me to leave the school and take over the land when he retires next year. Everyone in the village says a teacher's salary is small and the eldest son's place is on the farm. Some days I agree. Some days I feel like I'm betraying the kids.

Lakshmi rang tonight. She said, "Anna, why do you talk like you're two different people? You're a farmer who teaches. Or a teacher who farms."

It stuck.

So, a plan I want to show Appa on Sunday:
— Keep teaching weekdays.
— Weekends and holidays on the land, with the helper Appa already pays.
— Use our fields for a school garden project.

I don't know if Appa will agree. But it's the first plan that feels like me, not half of me.

Pradeep

14 May, Kheerganga base

Turned the group back at 11 a.m., two hours short of the pass. The forecast said 40 percent chance of storms after noon, and I could see cloud building over the ridge. Two of the guests were furious. One said I'd wasted their money.

By 2 p.m. the sky was completely clear. Of course it was.

Jyoti, my co-guide, found me sulking by the tents. "Would you make the same call again, with what you knew at eleven?"

I thought about it honestly. Yes. Forty percent is too high with slow walkers and one steep stretch. Clear skies now don't make the decision wrong; they make it lucky for everyone.

What I will change: check the forecast again at 9 instead of only at dawn, and explain the risk to guests before we start, so turning back isn't a shock.

Still annoyed. But not doubting the call.

Omkar

qa.a: The forecast said 40 percent chance of storms after noon.

qa.a: Omkar felt annoyed and sulky, second-guessing the choice after guests were furious.

qa.a: Omkar will recheck the forecast at 9 and explain the risk to guests at the start, so decisions use fresher information and surprise the group less.

In Ramesh's village near Wardha, everyone was sowing soybean again. The radio said the monsoon might be normal; the extension officer said it might be late. Nobody knew.

Ramesh walked his four acres with Ojas, his friend from agriculture college, who now worked at the block office.

"If the rain is good, soybean pays best," Ojas said. "If it's late, you could lose the lot."

"And tur?"

"Handles a dry spell better. Pays less if the rain is good."

Ramesh chewed a grass stem. "Then I'll put three acres in soybean and one in tur. If I'm wrong, I'm only a bit wrong."

His uncle laughed at him. "Half-hearted farmer."

The rains came on time and were generous. Soybean did well; the tur acre earned less. At the tea shop, his uncle teased him again.

Ramesh just shrugged. "I didn't know in June what I know now. I'd split it again."

The promotion email arrived at four: Lakshmi would be head chef. Aadhya read it twice on the kitchen tablet, then put it face down.

At six, a 300-plate wedding order was due, and two cooks had called in sick.

Aadhya's jaw ached from clenching. She had been at the hotel a year longer. She had trained Lakshmi on the tandoor. Lakshmi walked in, saw her face, and hesitated.

For a moment Aadhya wanted to say something cutting. Instead she went into the cold store, stood among the crates for sixty seconds, and breathed.

When she came out, she said, "Congratulations. Tell me where you want me tonight."

Lakshmi looked relieved. "Can you run the grill line? You're faster than me there."

They got the order out by nine. Afterwards, Aadhya wrote a note to herself: ask the manager what I need for the next opening. Then she went home and cried in the auto, which was allowed.

In the logistics office in Ho Chi Minh City, Nadia's desk faced the river, but she rarely looked at it. Her job was the weekly shipping report, and for three months the company's AI assistant had drafted it for her in ten minutes.

On Thursday, she noticed the container count for Da Nang looked high. The assistant had counted a cancelled shipment twice. The report had already gone to her manager, Bao, in draft.

Her stomach dropped. She went straight to his desk. "The draft has an error. It's mine to fix, not the tool's. I didn't check the cancellations."

Bao nodded slowly. "Good that you caught it. What will you change?"

"I'll check every total against the booking system before sending. And once a month, I'll do the whole report by hand, so I don't forget how."

Bao smiled. "Write that down for the team. They're all using it."

Subject: How we use the coding assistant (proposal)

Hi Divyansh and team,

After last week's outage, I've been thinking about how we use the AI coding assistant. To be clear: the bug was in code I approved. The assistant wrote it, but my name was on the review.

So here's what I'd like us to try from Monday:

1. Anything the assistant writes gets reviewed like a junior's code. No "it looks fine".
2. Every AI-generated function needs a test we write ourselves.
3. On Fridays, pick one small task and do it without the assistant. Divyansh, I know you'll groan. But I noticed I couldn't remember how to write a basic query last month, and that scared me.

Let's discuss at stand-up. Tell me if any of this feels unworkable.

Thanks,
Samir

That night he made choices, not rules. He kept one news source, read once in the morning. He deleted two feeds entirely and moved the others off his home screen. He left six group chats and muted five. He kept the family chat.

The drums were harder. He asked Tenzin to practise after seven, and Tenzin agreed if Ujjwal bought the earplugs.

The next week, the wifi still dropped. But when it did, Ujjwal kept translating from the printed pages. He finished two days early, and on the last evening he went to Tenzin's gig without taking a single photo.

qa.q: How many times had Ujjwal checked his phone before lunch on Monday?
qa.a: He had checked his phone ninety times before lunch.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt after counting ninety checks?
qa.a: Ujjwal was probably shocked and frustrated, realising how much the phone was eating into limited time before the deadline.

qa.q: Which of Ujjwal's choices could others try, and why do they work?
qa.a: Keeping one news source once a day and removing feeds from the home screen work because they cut the default pull without banning everything.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see the changes in the flat?
qa.a: Tenzin had to shift drum practice, but got earplugs and a flatmate who came to the gig and was fully present.

grounding: Under a deadline in a noisy flat, a young translator chooses which apps and news to keep deliberately instead of by default.

Pooja noticed it on a Sunday in Chennai: she had spent forty minutes in bed watching strangers' kitchen makeovers, and she didn't even want a new kitchen.

She sat up. "Darshan, how many apps do you think I actually chose?"

Her husband looked up from the newspaper. "Chose?"

"Most of them I downloaded because someone said to. Or they came on the phone."

That week she went through them one by one. For each, she asked: do I use this on purpose, or does it use me? She kept the maps, banking, the family chat and a language-learning app she genuinely liked. She deleted the video app and switched her screen to greyscale in the evenings.

She also subscribed to the paper newspaper Darshan read, instead of three news feeds.

The first few evenings, she kept reaching for the phone and finding nothing interesting. By the third week, she was reading a novel on the balcony, and Darshan had quietly started doing greyscale too.

qa.q: What was Pooja watching for forty minutes in bed?
qa.a: She was watching strangers' kitchen makeovers.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel during the first few evenings after deleting the apps?
qa.a: Pooja felt restless and a bit bored, still reaching for the phone out of habit and finding nothing.

qa.q: What question did Pooja use to choose her tools, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked whether she uses each app on purpose or it uses her, which helps separate chosen tools from default ones.

qa.q: How is Darshan affected by Pooja's changes?
qa.a: Darshan was puzzled at first, but gets a companion for the newspaper and quietly copies the greyscale habit himself.

grounding: A young woman reviews her apps and news sources and keeps only the ones she uses on purpose.

In Kalimpong, news travels by the evening bus. When Dolma's neighbour, Mrs. Rai, was taken to Siliguri with a heart problem, the whole lane heard that the family had sold their land to pay the hospital.

Dolma, a primary teacher, lay awake that night. She had no health cover apart from a small school scheme she had never read.

On Saturday, she and Shreya, who taught Class 4, sat on the staffroom bench with Dolma's school papers. The scheme covered very little. Neither of them understood half the words.

"My uncle's friend is a licensed insurance adviser in town," Shreya said. "He explained my father's policy properly."

Dolma went with a list of questions: what was covered, what wasn't, whether her mother could be included. She took the brochures home and read the exclusions twice, and did not sign that day.

Two weeks later, she chose a family health plan. She told Mrs. Rai's daughter about the adviser too.

qa.q: What did Dolma take home and read twice?
qa.a: She took the brochures home and read the exclusions twice.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling the night after hearing about the Rai family?
qa.a: Dolma felt worried and uneasy, realising she had almost no health cover and had never read her school scheme.

qa.q: Which of Dolma's steps are sensible when choosing insurance?
qa.a: She checked her existing cover, went to a licensed adviser with questions, read the exclusions, and took time instead of signing the same day.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Rai's daughter feel when Dolma tells her about the adviser?
qa.a: She might feel grateful and a little hopeful, having seen what a lack of cover cost her family.

grounding: In a small town, a young teacher reviews her insurance after a neighbour's crisis and chooses adequate cover with a qualified adviser.

passage:
Alejandro had worked at the design studio in Valencia for eight months before Yara, eating lunch beside him on the terrace, asked, "Did you sign up for the pension plan?"

"I'm twenty-four," he said. "Retirement is for people with grey hair."

"The company adds money when you do," Yara said. "If you don't join, you don't get it."

He went back to his desk, curious and slightly annoyed. He found the plan booklet in an old HR email. It was long and full of terms he didn't know.

So he booked a meeting with the HR officer, who explained how the plan worked, and suggested he talk to an independent adviser about how much would suit him. Alejandro did both.

That Friday he signed up. It felt strange, like writing a letter to an old man he hadn't met. At lunch he told Yara. She raised her coffee cup. "To grey-haired Alejandro."

qa.q: Where did Alejandro find the plan booklet?
qa.a: He found the plan booklet in an old HR email.

qa.q: How did Alejandro feel after Yara asked about the pension plan?
qa.a: Alejandro felt curious and slightly annoyed, perhaps a bit embarrassed to have ignored it for eight months.

qa.q: What steps did Alejandro take to understand the plan?
qa.a: He read the booklet, met the HR officer and talked to an independent adviser before signing up.

qa.q: How does Yara see Alejandro signing up?
qa.a: Yara is pleased and amused, glad that her lunchtime question led him to act.

grounding: A young worker abroad learns about his workplace retirement plan and starts saving after getting help from HR and an adviser.

The junior engineer's quarters in the district town of Hingoli had a small porch and a scooter parked on it. Siddharth had been posted there for a year, and the scooter did everything he needed.

Then his cousin's wedding came. At the reception, relatives asked, "Still on a scooter? A government engineer?" One uncle said a big SUV would bring better marriage proposals.

On the drive home in a borrowed car, Siddharth felt small, then irritated at himself for feeling small.

He called his friend Hrithik from college. "Tell me honestly. Am I being stingy?"

Hrithik laughed. "Do you need a car for work?"

"The department gives me a jeep for site visits."

"Then you need a car for the wedding season. That's not a need, that's a costume."

Siddharth laughed too. He kept the scooter. When his pay went up that April, he left the extra in savings and bought his mother the reading glasses she had been putting off.

qa.q: What does the department give Siddharth for site visits?
qa.a: The department gives him a jeep for site visits.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel on the drive home from the reception?
qa.a: Siddharth felt small and embarrassed by the relatives' comments, then irritated with himself for caring.

qa.q: How did Hrithik help Siddharth separate need from image?
qa.a: He asked whether a car was needed for work, and when it wasn't, pointed out the car would only be for show.

qa.q: How might the relatives see Siddharth's choice to keep the scooter?
qa.a: Some relatives may still think it looks odd for a government engineer, as they judge by status rather than by what he needs.

grounding: A young engineer in a small town resists pressure to buy a status car and keeps spending on needs, not image.

After her promotion in Seoul, Soo-ah noticed the bags. Every woman in the new team carried one of three famous designer handbags. Hers was canvas, from a street market in her university days.

At dinner, she said to Wei, "I think I should buy one. It's like a uniform."

Wei, cutting kimchi pancake, asked, "Did anyone say anything?"

"No. But I feel them looking."

"Or you feel yourself looking."

She was quiet. It was true that no one had mentioned it.

That weekend she walked through the department store and stood in front of the bags for a long time. The price was more than her raise for three months. She thought about the trip to visit her grandmother in Busan that she kept postponing.

She walked out without one, a little sad and a little proud. On Monday, she carried the canvas bag. At lunch, a senior colleague asked where she had got it. "My university market," she said. "Ten years ago."

qa.q: What kind of bag did Soo-ah carry?
qa.a: Her bag was canvas, from a street market in her university days.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah feel walking out of the department store?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt a little sad and a little proud, having chosen what she valued over fitting in.

qa.q: What helped Soo-ah decide against the bag?
qa.a: Checking whether anyone had actually commented and comparing the price with the trip to visit her grandmother helped her separate image from needs.

grounding: After a promotion abroad, a young woman resists a status purchase by separating image from what she truly values.

"They want to turn half the park into a parking lot," Keerthana said, holding up the ward notice. "Half!"

Tarun, reading over her shoulder, frowned. "But the lane is always blocked. Ambulances can't get through."

"So we lose the only green space for cars?"

"I'm just saying there's a problem on both sides."

Keerthana sat down on the steps of the ward office. "Fine. What's in the notice exactly?"

Tarun read aloud. "Public meeting, Saturday, ten o'clock. Residents can submit written suggestions until the 20th."

"So it's not decided."

They spent the evening walking the lane and counting parked cars, then the park at dusk, counting children. On Saturday, Keerthana spoke for two minutes. "We counted forty-two cars and sixty children. Could the council consider parking on the empty plot behind the market, and keep the park?"

I used to think public consultations were theatre. Decisions made, officials nodding. Then the city proposed moving our bus stop half a kilometre, and I went, mostly to complain.

The municipal officer, Thomas, showed a map. The current stop sat right at a blind curve; there had been three accidents in two years. The new spot was safer, but further for older people in our lane.

I stood up anyway and said it was unfair to the elderly. Thomas didn't argue. He asked, "What would make the new stop workable for them?"

I didn't have an answer. I went home annoyed, then slowly curious.

That week I spoke to six older neighbours. Most said the walk was fine if there was a shelter and a bench halfway. I wrote that up, one page, and emailed it before the deadline.

The bench arrived four months later. I'm Bidisha, and I've learnt that policy is mostly trade-offs, and that questions get further than slogans.

qa.q: How many accidents had there been at the current stop?
qa.a: There had been three accidents in two years.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel after Thomas's question at the consultation?
qa.a: Bidisha felt annoyed and caught out at first, then slowly curious about what would actually work.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do that made participation useful?
qa.a: Bidisha spoke to six older neighbours, found out what they needed, and sent a short written proposal before the deadline.

qa.q: How might the older neighbours see the new bench?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and listened to, since the bench made the longer walk to the safer stop manageable.

grounding: A young adult learns about the trade-offs in a local bus stop decision and participates constructively in the consultation.

passage:
Gram sabha note, Saturday — Francis, panchayat secretary.

The main item was the water tank schedule. For months, the upper hamlet has had water only two days a week, and complaints have been loud and angry.

Chandrika, who works as a data entry operator in town and comes home on weekends, asked to speak. She had a notebook. She had recorded, for a month, when water came to each hamlet and for how long. The upper hamlet was getting less than half the hours of the lower one, because the valve is opened in order of distance.

She did not accuse anyone. She said, "I understand the pump can't run longer; the electricity is limited. Could the order change every week?"

Some elders frowned at a young woman speaking so long. But the numbers were clear. The sabha voted to rotate the valve order for a trial month.

I have asked Chandrika to keep recording.

qa.q: How long did Chandrika record the water timings?
qa.a: She had recorded, for a month, when water came to each hamlet and for how long.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt when some elders frowned at her?
qa.a: Chandrika may have felt nervous or uncomfortable, but determined enough to keep presenting her numbers calmly.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's contribution constructive?
qa.a: She gathered real data, accepted the limit on electricity, avoided blame, and proposed a simple change to try.

qa.q: How might the families in the upper hamlet see the vote?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and hopeful that someone listened, after months of getting less water.

grounding: A panchayat secretary notes a young woman using data to understand a trade-off and help the gram sabha agree a fairer water schedule.
